There are many reasons why I particularly avoid Korean films, yet I do not detest them entirely. One of the biggest factors is their tendency toward exaggerated theatricality at the expense of a tighter logical structure in the plots they follow. Park-Chan Wook is the most classic example of this phenomenon of Korean cinema with his films such as Oldboy where he tries to tie out a similar moral tragedy like the Danish film Jagten (2012) through a stylistically elaborate revenge spiral, but the plot eventually moves beyond the boundaries of grounded internal logic. Devices such as hypnosis can feel like one-time narrative bandages, introduced primarily to connect pieces that otherwise resist being connected. My problem isn't simply that Oldboy is unrealistic, it's that, for me, certain revelations and mechanisms feel retroactively installed to preserve a plot that has already stretched beyond its own credibility. The Handmaiden is also a victim of a massive twisted theatrical presentation with an underwhelming logical ground for plot. So are many many films such as I Saw The Devil, A Bittersweet Life, Forgotten etc... Decision To Leave is what I consider the most perfect Park-Chan Wook film and what I consider the film where he establishes a perfect route between a top-notch presentation, poetic moral complexity and an established ground of logic that complements the plot. The Wailing is no stranger to this victimisation but deliberately worse. Here we follow the story of a dad, who is a police in a remote town, where the guilty, the misdeeds, the victims and even the apparent solutions reveal themselves so early, yet the plot repeatedly demands that its characters descend further into its catacombs of uncertainty, not necessarily because the logic requires it, but because the theatrical experience does with its top-of-the-class cinematography, set design and the quote-unquote "thriller" ride of Korean cinema which is deemed to be so extraordinarily unique. Even the 2 hour 40 minutes runtime serves the furthest from being a momentum of an intrigued continuity. Instead, the film repeatedly pauses, expands, and obscures itself in pursuit of an exhilarating theatrical experience, backed by extraordinary cinematography and production design, but without enough narrative momentum to justify the journey. It could be a brilliant concept film, if only it was told with a better expression of plot in mind, better attachment of all the fragmentations of the elements since they were so obviously present. Yet none clicks except until the final reveal becomes the most emphasized point of the film. In short, my utmost frustration is specifically with the film's prolonged withholding of decisive movement. Underwhelming is an understatement for The Wailing. Bong Joon Ho is the only Korean director to ever do Korean cinema the justice of the trio- cinematic experience, established complementary logic and an unique narrative statement of being a Korean foreign cinema. Lee Chang Dong also comes to mind. Burning is my most favorite Korean cinema of all time. I just want to say this phenomenon is of course not exclusive to Korean cinema only. Any film can become a victim of its own grandiosity when cinematic spectacle begins demanding sacrifices from the internal logic that is supposed to sustain it. I'm looking right at you Amadeus .

One of the things I like about Korean movies is that the stories are usually quite different from the usual stuff. Even when the movie isn’t particularly great, the ideas are often different enough to keep me interested. The Wailing has a really good opening. The mystery behind the deaths and the strange behaviour of the people really pulled me in. I kept watching because I wanted to know what was going on. Up until around the middle, it just kept getting stranger and stranger. But after that, everything starts becoming a complete mess. Is it a ghost? Poisonous mushrooms? Zombies? A demon? A curse? Black magic? Damn, my brain was getting tired trying to figure it out. 😂 Then there’s the shaman’s “healing ritual” with all that dancing and jumping around. And apparently the devil knows how to use a camera to take pictures for black magic too. OMG… this movie really went everywhere. The Korean mountain village setting is beautiful, but I just can’t get along with the story. For me, the beginning until the middle is good. After that, it completely falls apart. Not recommended.

In Asia il coesistere di giallo e paranormale nella stessa storia ha un carattere diverso da quello che possiamo trovare in Sherlock o altri racconti occidentali. Lo spiritismo spesso si assimila alle indagini come un dato plausibile e popolarmente creduto, almeno nei villaggi più rurali. Goksung parte molto bene, la prima parte è un crime a tinte mostruose, inspiegabili, che sono proprio l'aspetto più avvincente, perché spingono a voler sapere cosa ci può essere dietro gli efferati omicidi. Per tutta la durata del film, nel totale un po' troppo prolungata, la fotografia va migliorando, diventando pian piano più fredda, come se un'occulta entità diabolica si stesse impossessando della stessa atmosfera, mentre per quanto riguarda la storia la seconda parte vede incrinarsi  la componente misteriosa per schiaffarti in volto la verità. In questa parte prende vigore la parte religiosa del film, tra esorcisti, citazioni bibliche al canto del gallo e altro che giustifica la citazione evangelica a Luca all'inizio del film, ma con ciò si assiste anche all'indiscreto farsi protagonista del gore, all'indebolimento del ritmo investigativo, alla banalizzazione della storia, che di originale ha solo ciò che riguarda la tradizione coreana a noi sconosciuta, e a scene che non hanno l'impatto desiderato, come il rituale sciamanico per liberare la figlia, un costante battere di percussioni e grida senza climax ascendente. Il buon regista tiene in piedi l'impianto fino al termine, ma lo script a mio parere non fa altrettanto, non per difetti oggettivi ma per scelte talvolta imperfette.

"O Lamento" é um suspense com potencial que se estende além do necessário. Esse é mais um longa sul-coreano de Na Hong-jin que mistura elementos do terror e suspense em torno de Jong-Goo, um policial de uma pequena cidade que investiga mortes misteriosas em seu vilarejo. O que parecia epidemia ganha contornos sobrenaturais e religiosos conforme sua filha apresenta sintomas estranhos. A premissa é sólida e o diretor faz questão de marcar presença, mas o filme carrega consigo um problema estrutural que o compromete: é longo demais para a ideia que sustenta. O filme possui um bom clima de suspense, porém a duração não ajuda, poderia ter sido mais enxuto, e se perde às vezes no roteiro deixando o espectador impaciente. Há momentos onde a câmera trabalha com precisão, onde o diretor demonstra sensibilidade visual genuína ao filmar os rituais e a tensão entre personagens. A estrutura religiosa do filme oferece camadas interessantes, mas Na Hong-jin não consegue contê-las adequadamente dentro de 156 minutos. O roteiro flerta com devaneio total em seus segmentos intermediários, explorando filosofia religiosa quando deveria intensificar a narrativa principal. Algumas atuações carecem de sutileza, especialmente em momentos que exigem nuance emocional, o que prejudica a credulidade de cenas críticas. O melhor que o filme oferece existe em seu final. A última meia hora confunde o espectador e o deixa cheio de dúvidas, com reviravoltas e um final surpreendente. É quando Na Hong-jin finalmente alinha visão e execução, permitindo que a ambiguidade moral do desfecho respire adequadamente. Nesse segmento, o diretor comprova que possui potencial genuíno para manipular emocões e conceitos complexos. Porém, tudo o que precede essa conclusão deveria ter sido trabalhado com maior economia narrativa. Certamente é um filme de ideias contidas demais numa estrutura que não sabe dizer não, logo, não entendo o alvoroço em torno dele.

And Ari wept Quite the wild romp upon an initial viewing, even now I still remember how distributed Jong-goo finding those photos made me feel. Regretfully though this wound up being less riveting  conceptually after a much delayed rewatch. Now in saying that I’m not claiming it's entirely void of any non-cinematic merit. With a much better understanding of Korea’s antipathy towards Japan due to their colonialist occupation during the early 20th century helps illuminate Gokseong’s central subtext ( or just text now ) in a very appreciated manner. This makes a lotta the “clues,” “hints” or actions of Kunimura Jun’s character, aptly named Japanese Man , click for me. Our character's treatment of him, however “justified” in the context of the film's spiritual battle between light and dark, is painted in a far more tragic light by the end. Jong-goo , the village, and by extension us are given divine punishment for blind discrimination. This helps make the ending, one which I found quite frustrating on a first watch, ring rather potent. What we see and what is actually there are two different things and believing that isn’t true is a dangerous belief to hold. The wider issue for myself is the film doesn’t always compel and thus my mind occasionally tends to wander here or there. Could this’ve been remedied by trimming it down a tad? Yea maybe but even then it’s so clearly a fully realized vision that I can’t help but still admire the ambition. Certain leaps in logic might be perplexing if not for the fact the film actively acknowledges them in a manner less irksome and more cheeky fudging of plausibility. I will say it helps that this film still looks euphoric. Splendid mountainscapes made of croaked bark and rough rock all doused in a healthy hue of blue and orange make their harboring of poisonous beasts feel all the more enticing. Again, not an all timer for me but far from being a foul film.

“Not everything that moves, breathes, and talks is alive. Countless people have perished because they didn't understand that.” Despite all the ways in which horror is often derided as a simplistic genre, dismissed as derivative or exploitative, horror can in fact be complex and multifaceted. Horror can be many things, because, obviously, many things can be horrific. Na Hong-jin’s sprawling supernatural horror mystery hybrid The Wailing is, indeed, many things. Maybe even many different types of movies. Part village noir, part police procedural, part family drama, part supernatural mystery, part folk horror, and, at one point, even a zombie film, before eventually descending into demonic possession and madness, Na’s film refuses to settle comfortably into any one genre. If there was ever a modern horror film that felt like Bong Joon-ho's Memories of Murder by way of Henry James’s The Turn of the Screw (hell, maybe even Mikhail Bulgakov’s The Master and Margarita ), then this is it. Which may frustrate just as many as it captivates. The Wailing is a truly ambitious slice of horror, where a bumbling policeman, who is also plagued by recurring nightmares, investigates a series of mysterious killings and illnesses in his remote Korean village. But when his own daughter begins exhibiting the same disturbing symptoms, what begins as an investigation quickly becomes a desperate attempt to save her. Yet, by shifting from grotesque to funny, back to frightening, and finally to despairing, The Wailing 's slow descent into paranoia and horror is a rather winding road, one that takes some truly unexpected turns along the way (the lightning strike), but somehow remains remarkably cohesive. Here is a film that (much like what Lincoln Michel of GQ wrote) mixes the supernatural and the mundane, blending together ghosts, zombies, body horror, Eastern exorcism, Christian mythology, demonic curses, creepy children, police procedural, medical thriller, and much, much more into a narrative that, by the end, somehow coalesces and works. It's a lot for a horror film, but The Wailing pulls it off. In essence, it's a horror film that seemingly keeps shifting the nature of its horror, a sprawling horror mystery that refuses to be neatly pinned down, because such ambiguity and confusion is the devil's playground. What begins as intriguing, even oddly comical at times, eventually becomes outright horrific, as if some cosmic deity with a warped sense of humor has taken a personal vendetta against these people, infecting the community with an evil that nobody can quite understand, because no one is ever entirely sure what that evil actually is. And like what good horror should do, but so rarely does, Na constructs his film to leave you with more questions than answers, slowly springing an ambiguous bleakness upon the audience the deeper they venture into its mystery. Which is awesome, even if many might complain about its sprawling narrative. Perhaps The Wailing could have lost 20 minutes from its whopping 156-minute runtime (which, unless you're The Shining , is long for any horror film), or that its sprawling, ambiguous narrative could have been tightened or presented in a less obfuscated manner. Maybe some things are lost in translation or cultural differences. But Na Hong-jin takes his time, and The Wailing is better off for it, allowing everything to unfold in a deliberate, if at times eccentric, manner that gives his film the feeling of a family epic told by way of supernatural horror. The Wailing blends all of these elements into something that feels original and unpredictable, while every actor grounds its increasingly bizarre turns in recognizably human fear and desperation. Horror is rarely epic, since the genre works best when it operates on an intimate level, but The Wailing makes a pretty compelling case for why it can be. Sprawling yet still atmospherically intimate. The Wailing is a good one. It took me ten years to finally watch it, but I now understand why Ari Aster has called it one of his favorite modern horror films. The influence on Hereditary seems obvious, especially in the way both transform family tragedy into something increasingly horror and incomprehensible. “But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit. And he said to them, ‘Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.’ -Luke 24:34-37” Been a hot minute since I’ve watched a film and I got back into it with a banger. Imagine the father-daughter relationship in Train to Busan combined with the supernatural levels of horror and thrill from The Exorcist and mixed with the history and culture of Korean shamanism from Exhuma. Now give that steroids and you got The Wailing . Upon watching this film, I have way more questions than I had as I was watching it. To be honest, I actually don’t know what happened. For such a huge chunk of the film, I’ve been led to believe that the old Japanese man was some sort of demonic power that casted a sinister shadow over the Korean village (probably inspired by anti-Japanese sentiment from Koreans due to colonization, just like in Exhuma ). There were so many clues that hinted that that likelihood, especially when the dad cop barges into the Japanese man’s house and found those disgusting pictures and shrines. It was as clear as day that the old man was responsible. There was no other way around. Even the shaman confirmed that, as he describes the old Japanese man as a fisher, casting a line out into the water and baits anyone that fall for his schemes. And the pinnacle of this growing suspicion is the simultaneous rituals, which masterfully showcased a battle of spirits for the daughter’s life and essence (arguably my favorite sequence in the film. It was gripping, intense, and thrilling). And then all of a sudden, just like that, everything comes crashing down because the shaman is confronted by the woman in the white robes and then calls the dad cop, frantically telling him that she was responsible and that the old man was another shaman combating her. Then we’re in a standoff between the woman in white and the shaman, where she’s telling the dad cop that she set a trap for the demon at his house and that he needs to wait and the shaman is saying that she’s lying and that dad cop needs to get back. But the woman is wearing articles of clothing from the victims so that’s a clear giveaway. Meanwhile the priest goes on to find the Japanese man in a cave and he reveals that he’s the devil and responsible for terrorizing the village, to which he takes pictures of the priest. And just when it can’t get any more confusing, the shaman returns to the dad cop’s house to find everyone slaughtered but then takes out a camera, photographs the dead, and then puts the pictures in a box filled with the pictures of all the other dead victims. So there are 3 entities that are potentially responsible and the film ends on an ambiguous note that doesn’t resolve the conflict. Instead, the film ends on a happier note of the dad remembering the happy times with his daughter as he’s dying by her hand. Like what just happened 😂 I actually like and appreciate the fact that the truth never reveals itself. With every plot twist and then, our sense of reality and truth gradually becomes more distorted, completely and intentionally shattering any truth and objectivity that would remain as the film went on. And to be honest, I actually don’t want to know who was the real villain or not because I feel like it would diminish the objective the film, which is more than capably achieved. This was my firs t나홍진 film and the style is so right up my alley. Not only was the cinematography exquisite in capturing the beauty of the Korean countryside, but much of his style was cinematically intentional and exact. He guides audiences towards what he wants us to see and not see through frames within frames. Almost every focal point in each scene was enclosed in a frame within the actual frame, which makes us think about who to follow and how to follow the story. I thought that was executed very well. My only complaint is that the dialogue was almost to the point of being completely incomprehensible. Because this film took place in the Korean countryside, these are country folk and they have 사투리, which means accent/dialect and their vocab and dictation is completely different than that of city folk in Seoul and Incheon. So I actually couldn’t make out what they were really saying but that’s a minor nitpick in a major banger. Way more sinister than I was expecting. Gritty, disturbing, and aggressive, just the way I like films (sometimes).

Maybe it's because only "the best of the best" makes it over here to America, but it feels like Korean filmmakers really know how to make incredible detective stories (Memories of Murder) and horror movies (Train to Busan and Exhuma). The Wailing combines both and makes an incredible film noir, meets folk horror film. The wailing exceeds at making you feel uncomfortable, there are certainly movies that are more intense, more unrelenting and/or more brutal, but few movies make my skin crawl in the way The Wailing does. It's fast and intense when it needs to be and it lets you sit long and slowly with the disturbing material it's presenting you. Its folk horror aspects also take parts of Korean spiritualism and culture and makes them digestible to those of us who are unfamiliar. The police procedural and detective parts are engaging and keep you guessing throughout. The characters are handled very well, especially as we watch the family of our main protagonist struggle and then have to face suppernatural forces. The Wailing really balances things incredibly well when you consider it's a family drama, police procedural, folk horror. That's a lot for one movie to take on, but it does it phenominally well and parts of it will stick with you for years to come.

disfruto tanto cuando el género del horror está bien hecho que terminas al final de la película tan satisfecho. esta cinta no se queda atrás, con una apuesta que yo podría comparar con una escalera que te lleva a distintas experiencias. hablaba de que esta película la comparo con una suerte de escalera que te lleva a diferentes ambientes, puesto que tú miras el título e investigas el género de esta y, claro, es horror. sabemos cómo lo hacen, ya está totalmente sobrevalorado. ahora, con esta película es distinto: acá se rompen las reglas, partiendo con una trama orientada al humor negro, y esto se conjuga tan bien porque, a pesar de que estaban aconteciendo cosas más allá de la explicación humana, los personajes se mantienen ignorantes a esta realidad. pero, de a poco, se va generando esta introspección acerca de si es realmente lo que está ocurriendo relacionado con lo oculto, hasta que te das cuenta de que la realidad es mucho más oscura, pero lamentablemente no puedes hacer mucho. me gusta que en todo el filme se dé pie a decisiones que son muy humanas, lo que significa dejarte llevar por lo que te dicta tu corazón, aunque eso realmente no sea lo que define una acción o decisión correcta. a través de esto, el protagonista y la trama juegan con el espectador, tratando de hacerte detective sobre quién es realmente el antagonista. ¿hay realmente uno? ¿es verídico seguir tus instintos o tomarás una decisión que acabará con tu vida y la de tus seres más queridos? una de esas películas que demuestran por qué el horror todavía puede sorprender. juega con distintos géneros, mantiene la tensión y te hace cuestionar todo hasta el último momento. una experiencia redonda y, para mí, prácticamente perfecta.
